content.title: About
content.content: Turkey fat is the fat from turkey, collected from the skin and body cavity and often rendered into a clear, soft cooking fat. It has a mild poultry flavor and is used for roasting, frying, and flavoring dishes, and for basting poultry. Like other poultry fats, it is softer at room temperature than beef or mutton fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey fat is a by-product of roasting or butchering turkey and can be rendered into a clear fat.
Poultry fats are softer at room temperature than beef or mutton fats because they contain more unsaturated fat.
Turkey fat is often saved from the roasting pan to make gravy or to cook vegetables and potatoes.
It has a moderate smoke point and a mild poultry flavor.
Rendered poultry fats such as schmaltz have been used in Jewish and Eastern European cooking for generations.

items.title: Concentrated energy
items.content: Turkey fat is a calorie-dense source of energy.

items.title: Mostly unsaturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef and mutton fat, turkey fat contains more unsaturated fat.

items.title: Adds flavor
items.content: A small amount adds richness and savory flavor to roasted vegetables, potatoes, and grains.

items.title: Contains fat-soluble vitamins
items.content: Turkey fat contains small amounts of vitamin E and vitamin A.

items.title: Cooking versatility
items.content: It can be used for roasting, sautéing, and basting.

items.title: High in calories and saturated fat
items.content: Turkey fat is calorie-dense and still contains saturated fat, so portions should be small.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: Animal fats contain cholesterol, which matters for people with certain health conditions.

items.title: Overheating and reuse
items.content: Heating fat past its smoke point or reusing it many times can produce harmful compounds and bad flavors.

items.title: Spoilage and allergies
items.content: Poultry fat can spoil and turn rancid, and people with poultry allergy should avoid it.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use turkey fat in small amounts to roast potatoes and vegetables, sauté, make gravy, or baste poultry. It can be rendered by slowly melting trimmed fat and straining it. Use it in moderation and avoid heating it until it smokes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store rendered turkey fat in an airtight container in the refrigerator for a few weeks or freeze it for several months. Keep it away from light and heat. Discard fat that smells rancid, sour, or off.
